claims.text: Hardness and strength in single-phase high-entropy alloys are governed by atomic-scale lattice distortion.
Severe atomic-size mismatch among constituent elements causes atomic-scale lattice distortion.
Atomic-scale lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
The controlled material state is a single-phase FCC or BCC solid solution with a random distribution of constituent elements.
Atomic-size mismatch will be varied by substituting elements having different atomic radii while maintaining high compositional entropy.
Samples will receive identical thermal and mechanical histories to make their microstructures comparable.
Atomic-scale lattice distortion can be quantified using diffraction-derived lattice strain and pair-distribution-function analysis.
Local lattice distortions caused by atomic-size mismatch increase the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
An increased energy barrier for dislocation motion enhances hardness and strength.
Alloys with greater atomic-size mismatch will exhibit greater lattice distortion and dislocation pinning.
Alloys with greater atomic-size mismatch will exhibit higher hardness than alloys with smaller mismatch.
Alloys with greater atomic-size mismatch will exhibit higher strength than alloys with smaller mismatch.
A baseline HEA with minimal atomic-size mismatch will have lower lattice distortion.
A baseline HEA with minimal atomic-size mismatch will have lower hardness and strength.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase HEAs with random atomic distributions and without significant secondary phases, grain-boundary effects, or segregation.
Electronic effects and short-range ordering may also contribute to hardness and strength.
The hypothesis is falsified if greater atomic-size mismatch does not produce higher hardness and strength or if lattice distortion is uncorrelated with the measured mechanical properties.
